ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: raid points
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: How the storyteller decides how big the next raid will be
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Raid size is worked out from your wealth and colonists on the day the raid arrives.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every raid is bought with raid points. The storyteller adds points for your wealth and for your people, then scales the total by difficulty, by how old the colony is and by how well things have been going. This is why the raid after a big trade is larger. These figures may have shifted slightly in recent versions, so treat them as close guides.

li.heading: The formula
li.text: Raid points = (wealth points + pawn points) × difficulty × starting factor × adaptation factor. The result is never below 35 or above 10,000. The difficulty you picked sets one of the multipliers:
li.after: Some storytellers change the result after the cap. Randy Random multiplies it by anything from 50% to 150%.

li.heading: Wealth and people
li.text:
Wealth points are zero up to 14,000 colony wealth, then climb to 2,400 at 400,000, 3,600 at 700,000 and 4,200 at 1,000,000 and above. Items and creatures count in full, buildings at half. On top of that, each colonist adds pawn points: 15 while wealth is under 10,000, rising to 140 at 400,000 and 200 at 1,000,000.
The next raid is priced on what you own when it arrives, so watch your colony wealth before a big trade, loot haul or art spree. Idle silver, gold and art count toward wealth just the same as armor, weapons and medicine, but only the second kind helps you win the fight, so turn the one into the other. A tribal colony works by the same sums: its stone huts count at half value, and its stockpiles in full.

li.heading: Early days and adaptation
li.text:
Early raids come at a discount. The starting factor is 0.7 up to day 10 and rises to 1.0 by day 40, so have your defenses ready before day 40, when the discount runs out.
Adaptation follows how well things have been going. It starts at 0.8 and climbs while you avoid losses: 1.0 at 30 adaptation days and 1.2 at 60. In practice, 1.47 is the most you can reach.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: wealth and raid size
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What the storyteller counts toward raids, and what it barely notices
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Silver in the stockpile counts in full toward the next raid.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Not everything you own weighs the same when the storyteller prices a raid. Items and animals count in full, buildings at half, and each person counts according to their status and age. The cheapest way to keep raids manageable is to hold wealth in useful things and to add people who can fight.

li.heading: What counts, and how much

table.li: Buildings | Half their value; hit points are ignored
Tamed animals that can learn Attack | 8% of their combat power, whatever your wealth
Friendly mechs and entities | 20% at low wealth, 30% at 400,000, 40% at 1,000,000

li.after: The "wealth-independent progress" difficulty option stops wealth from driving raid size.

li.heading: Losses and loot
li.text: Losing people makes the next raids somewhat smaller. A colonist's death removes 30 adaptation days in a small colony (20 in a colony of 20), and a downed colonist removes 3.5 to 8. Bigger raids don't keep bringing better loot, either: what raiders carry stops getting better past 4,000 raid points.

li.heading: Where to keep your wealth
li.text:
Sell or use the piles of silver, gold and art you don't need before the next raid is priced on them. Walls and defenses are a better place for it: at half value, a stone wall adds few raid points for the protection it gives, so build the ones you need.
People are usually the best buy. A good fighter adds more defense than the pawn points they cost, so recruit them. Attack animals cost even less: at 8% of their combat power, they give a tribe without turrets extra fighters for very few raid points.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: how raids arrive
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Raiders are bought by combat power and come in several styles
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: The raid letter names the faction and how they are arriving.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The storyteller spends a raid's points on attackers, each with a combat power price. Most raiders walk in from the map edge, but some dig in with mortars, tunnel through your walls or drop out of the sky. Read the raid letter and note where they arrive before you decide where to fight.

li.heading: What the points buy
li.text:
A tribal villager costs 30 combat power, an archer 45, a warrior 50 and a hunter 60. A pirate drifter costs 35 and a scavenger 50; a scyther costs 150. The weakest raider costs 30. Sapper and center drop raids are smaller than their raid points suggest.
Human raiders fight until something breaks the raid, and pirates may give up and leave. Mechanoid raiders attack indefinitely, so against mechanoids bring EMP weapons and plan to destroy every one.

li.heading: Raid styles

table.li: Style | Where they appear | How to meet them
Assault | The map edge | Man your chokepoint
Siege | A camp being built | Break the camp or force the attack
Sappers, breachers | Through your walls | Wait behind inner walls
Center drop | Pods inside your walls | Spread out near cover
Scattered drop | Pods across the map | Spread out near cover

li.after: Manhunter packs are a separate threat with their own page. Tribal-level factions cannot use drop pods, but pirates and outlanders use them, so a tribe still has to prepare for pods and sieges.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: killboxes and chokepoints
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Make raiders walk one long path into your guns
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Raiders take the easiest open path, so make that path your killbox.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A chokepoint makes the raiders' easiest path a long corridor or a single doorway, so only a few of them can shoot at once while your people fight from cover. It is the cheapest defense in the game and works at any tech level. Sappers, breachers and drop pods ignore it, so keep a second line of defense inside the base.

li.heading: How raiders pick a path
li.text: Raiders take the easiest open route, however long. They break walls and doors only when no open way reaches your people. A trap they know about adds a path cost of 800 when they choose their way, and 40 when they step over it, so a heavily trapped lane can push them to another open way in. Sapper, smart and breaching raiders know where about 30% of your traps are, and a known trap never springs on them.

points.li: Leave one inviting entrance and close every other route with walls and doors. Nothing the raiders could smash may stand where they reach it from outside: a cooler in the outer wall, a lamp, a solar panel.
The entrance turns twice, then runs straight for four or five cells into the box, so a raider at the last corner can't see your shooters.
Keep the box and the doorway bare. Since 1.6 raiders stop and shoot from sandbags and barricades too.

Put the shooters straight across from the doorway, all within about 24° of its line and none right on it, more than 13.5 cells back against grenades. Each in a pocket (a wall in front, sandbags beside) has 75% cover; behind sandbags, 55%.
Line the outer stretch of the approach with traps and things that slow them, every other cell, keeping explosive traps away from where your own people will stand.
Keep an inner fallback line behind the first, round the bedrooms: breachers and sappers make for a bed.
Build it in stone, never wood. Things ignite above 235 °C and embers jump 2 tiles, so wood in a killbox is a fire trap for you.
Keep weapons and armor in an armory close to the line.

li.heading: Without turrets
li.text: Put archers behind sandbags or stone walls, and up to three melee fighters just outside a one-tile doorway, so raiders come through one at a time.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: cover
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What stops bullets, by how much, and from which angle
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Cover works best when the shot comes straight at it.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Cover lowers the chance a shot reaches whoever is behind it. How much depends on what the cover is, the angle of the shot and how close the shooter stands. Raiders use it as well as your colonists, so a tree in your firing lane gives them 25% cover.

li.heading: Cover values
li.after: Hit points decide how long the cover lasts: walls, sandbags, barricades and chunks have 300, doors 160 and rubble 50. Fence values are disputed. One list gives 25%; another gives fence gates 75% and ancient fences 55%.

li.heading: Angle and distance
li.text: Cover counts in full only when the shot comes nearly straight at it. The further the shot is off the line, the less it gives:

table.li: Angle off the line of fire | Cover counts

li.after: Only the eight cells around someone give them cover, and one on a diagonal counts as if the shot came at a wider angle than it does. Distance matters too. Cover only works at 33% when the shooter stands right in front of it, and at 67% from one tile away. Stop raiders before they reach your sandbags, with traps or melee fighters on the approach.

li.heading: Leaning out: the pocket
li.text:
Someone right behind a wall can't shoot through it, but with an open or sandbagged cell beside them they lean out into it to fire, and the game still reckons their cover from where they really stand. So a pocket, a piece of wall in front with sandbags at its front corners and beside it, gives 75% against a shot from straight ahead and 67 to 75% from the sides, more than any line of sandbags. Behind a wall with no room to lean, nobody shoots or is shot.
The same works for raiders: one at the corner of a wall leans out round it with the wall as cover. That's why a killbox's last turn is four or five cells before the box.

li.heading: Setting up a firing line
li.text: Put sandbags or barricades where your shooters stand, facing the expected approach head-on, or pockets where raiders must come straight at you. Before a raid, cut the trees and haul chunks and rubble out of your firing lanes. Sandbags and barricades need no power, so they are the backbone of any defense without turrets.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: traps
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Cheap single-use defenses, and the main defense of a colony without power
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Your own colonists spring a trap about 1 time in 200.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A trap fires once when a pawn steps on it, then must be rearmed or rebuilt. Enemies almost always set them off and your own people almost never do. For a colony without power, spike traps along the approach do much of a turret's job.

li.heading: Who sets them off

table.li: Enemies, including mechanoids and manhunting animals | 100%
Wild animals | 20% for spike traps, 5% for IEDs
Colonists, tame animals, slaves, friendly mechs | 0.5% (1 in 200)

li.after:
Nimble pawns are a tenth as likely to set one off. Sapper, smart and breaching raiders know about 30% of your traps and step around those.
Your own colonists can still spring a trap while uninstalling it, hauling on its tile or when you draft them onto it. Route drafted colonists around trap tiles, and keep haulers out of trap lanes with an allowed area.

li.heading: Spike traps and IEDs
li.text:
A wooden spike trap deals about 40 damage. Rebuild yours in steel or better once you have it to spare.
IEDs explode when bullets hit them, so keep them away from your firing positions and from walls you care about. Types include high-explosive, incendiary, EMP, firefoam, smoke and antigrain; tox needs Biotech and deadlife needs Anomaly.

li.heading: Laying them out
li.text:
Traps can't be built next to each other, diagonally either. A known trap adds a path cost of 800 when a raider chooses his way and 40 when he steps over it, so he goes round it if he can. Put them on the easy approach routes, and protect your own path with doors so raiders prefer the trapped one. Without power, line the corridor that leads to your doorway with spike traps, leaving a gap between each.
In a lane two wide, put a fence beside each trap: raiders who don't know the trap take its open side, and one who does has to climb the fence to get round it. Your own people, who know every trap, take the fence side. Keep IEDs at least five cells apart unless you want them to set each other off, and four or more from turrets and walls you care about.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: turrets
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Powered guns that need no colonist, and what they cost to keep
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Every turret you build adds to the size of the next raid.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Turrets give you guns that don't need a colonist, but every one needs power and steel to keep firing. They also add to your wealth and go silent in a solar flare. Use a few at your chokepoint to support your shooters, not as your whole defense.

li.heading: The three turrets
li.text: The mini-turret is weak, short-ranged, small and cheap. The uranium slug turret is slow and costly, with very high damage, range and accuracy. The autocannon turret in numbers:

li.heading: Keeping them firing
li.text:
Every turret needs power and uses resources to rearm; the cost depends on difficulty. Place turrets behind your chokepoint where your shooters can cover them, keep spare steel for rearming, and build only as many as your shooters can support and keep supplied. Turrets are buildings, so they count at half value toward raid strength.
A solar flare shuts every turret down. Arm your colonists as if the turrets weren't there, so a flare during a raid doesn't leave the line empty.

li.heading: Without power
li.text: Use spike traps, sandbags, archers behind cover and melee fighters at the door. Mortars need no power either, once researched.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: turret explosions
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Badly damaged turrets can blow up, so space them out
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A badly damaged autocannon turret gives about 4 seconds of warning before it explodes.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A badly damaged turret may explode a few seconds later and hurt everything nearby, including the next turret along. In a tight row, one explosion can set off the next turret and the one after it. Space them out and repair them between waves.

li.heading: What explodes, and how far

table.li: Autocannon turret | Below 20% health: a 50% chance, 240 ticks (about 4 seconds) later | 50 Bomb damage in a 5.9-tile radius
Mini-turret | Below 20% health: a 50% chance, 240 ticks later | 50 Bomb damage in a 3.9-tile radius
Mortar | Below a third of its health, it may explode | 50 Bomb damage in 4.9 tiles

li.after: Bomb damage is ×4 against walls and other solid structures (a wall takes 200, not the ×8 some guides give) and ×2 against buildings you can walk through, such as turrets, sandbags and traps. A 2x2 turret's blast is measured from its bottom-left cell.

li.heading: Spacing and repair
li.text:
Keep autocannon turrets about 6 tiles or more apart, so one blast can't reach the next, and mini-turrets 4 or more, which leaves 3 empty cells between them. A wall between two turrets stops the blast too. Keep turrets off wooden floors and away from where your colonists stand to fight, and repair any with a low health bar right after each wave.
IEDs behave the same way under fire: a stray bullet sets them off, so keep them clear of your own lines.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: mortars
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Map-wide artillery that needs no power, only a gunner and shells
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A mortar needs a gunner, shells and open sky, but no power.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A mortar can shell anywhere on the map, ignoring line of sight, as long as someone mans it. It is slow and inaccurate, but it is the best answer to a siege and to a mechanoid cluster you'd rather not walk up to. It needs no electricity, so a medieval colony can use one once it has the research.

li.heading: Getting one
li.text:
The mortar research costs 2,000, or 4,000 on a tribal start. A tribe should budget for it early, because a mortar is its only long-range answer to a siege.
Building one takes 50 metal (500 for small-volume metals), 1 reinforced barrel and 6 components, and 2,000 ticks of work at Construction 5. Mortars can't be bought. Each reinforced barrel lasts 20 shots, and sieges are a good source of barrels.

li.heading: Firing
li.text:
Range is 500 tiles, with a minimum of 29.9. Warm-up takes 240 ticks, and the cooldown of 1,680 ticks only counts down while the mortar is manned. Accuracy is poor, with a base miss radius of 9 tiles, so use several mortars and let their misses overlap on the target.
A mortar can't fire from under a roof, so build it in the open. Incoming shells are stopped only by overhead mountain.

li.heading: Shells
li.after: Use EMP shells on mechanoids and high-explosive on camps. Store shells in small stone rooms away from the mortars, so one hit doesn't set off the whole stack.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: sieges
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Raiders who dig in at the edge of the map and shell you
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A siege camp keeps getting fresh shells, so waiting it out doesn't work.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Siegers walk in from the map edge, have their supplies dropped in by pod, build sandbags and mortars, and shell your colony from a distance. The camp keeps getting resupplied and attacks after a few days anyway. Your chokepoint does nothing against shells, so you need to break the camp or make them attack early on your terms.

li.heading: How a siege goes
li.text:
The besiegers build sandbags and mortars, receive food and shells, and fire at colonists, buildings and other hostiles. Their shells are stopped only by overhead mountain; built roofs and thin rock roofs don't stop them. While the camp stands, keep colonists under overhead mountain or out of shell range.
They assault directly after a few days, as soon as their mortars are destroyed or can't be built, or after heavy casualties. Stealing a material they need, such as their components, can disrupt the siege.

li.heading: Breaking the camp

points.li: Shell the camp with your own mortars.
Snipe it with your longest-range gun to force an early assault. Without mortars or guns, provoke them with your longest bows.
Set off a psychic animal pulser.
Slip in and steal their components.

li.after: Whichever you choose, meet the assault at your chokepoint. Afterward, deconstruct or salvage what they leave: their mortars are a source of reinforced barrels.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: sappers and breachers
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Raiders who dig or smash through your walls instead of using the door
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Sappers dig toward your bedrooms, not your front gate.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Sappers dig through walls and rock to make the shortest route to a colonist's bedroom, ignoring your killbox entirely. Breachers smash any wall in their way instead of aiming for a particular spot. Either way, the fight happens inside your walls rather than at the gate.

li.heading: How they get in
li.text: Sappers mine or destroy walls to open the shortest route to a colonist's bedroom, and their groups are smaller than other raid types for the same raid points. Breachers attack walls in their path indiscriminately rather than targeting one spot. Sapper, smart and breaching raiders all know where about 30% of your traps are.

points.li: Leave an open route in, so the shortest path doesn't run through your bedrooms.
Make outer walls tough, and double important ones with a one-tile gap between them, so repairers aren't standing in the fire.
Keep shooters behind inner walls near the likely breach points.
Keep a mobile squad ready to intercept the group before it reaches the beds.
Without turrets, station melee fighters inside the wall nearest the bedrooms, with archers behind them.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: drop pod raids
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Raids that land by pod in the middle of your base or across the map
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Only overhead mountain stops a drop pod. Built roofs don't.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Drop pod raids skip the map edge. A center drop lands right on top of a colonist and attacks immediately; a scatter drop spreads its pods all over the map. Your killbox won't help, so your people need weapons and cover close to where they live and work.

li.heading: Where they land
li.text:
A center drop is centered on a colonist and attacks immediately. If you have an unroofed orbital trade beacon, it has a 40% chance to land on the beacon instead, so put the beacon somewhere you can defend, away from the bedrooms, or roof it. Center drop raids are smaller than their raid points suggest.
In a scatter drop the pods go haywire and land all across the map. Either kind breaks through built roofs and thin rock roofs, but not overhead mountain.

li.heading: Being ready
li.text:
Keep your people spread out near cover inside the base rather than bunched in one room, and store weapons near the living quarters, not only at the front gate.
Tribal-level factions cannot use drop pods, but even a tribe gets pods from pirates. Keep spears and bows within reach of the beds.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: manhunter packs
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Mad animals circle the base for a day or two, then wander off
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Manhunters can't open doors, but they will break one down to reach a colonist they saw go in.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A manhunter pack is a group of maddened animals that attacks any human it can reach. They can't open doors, so the safest answer is usually to stay inside and shoot from behind walls until they leave. The danger is the colonist caught outside, or the one who bolts indoors in plain sight.

li.heading: The pack
li.text: A pack gets 40% more points than a normal raid, and even a single animal can count as a pack. The species is picked from the local wildlife, limited to animals that can pass fences. The animals hang around the base for 24 to 54 in-game hours, then leave if they aren't killed. Animals killed while carrying scaria can rot instantly, which ruins the meat.

li.heading: When the letter arrives

points.li: Call colonists home right away, before the pack sees them.
Restrict everyone to an indoor allowed area until the pack leaves.
Shoot through a doorway or from behind walls, and let the traps do some work: manhunting animals trigger them 100% of the time.

li.after: The animals can't pass doors, but they will break one down if they see a colonist run behind it. Even a tribe with only bows does well here, because animals can't shoot back at a colonist behind a wall.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: mechanoid clusters
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A sleeping mechanoid base lands nearby; wake it on your terms
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A proximity activator wakes the cluster when a human comes within about 13 tiles.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A mechanoid cluster drops a small fortified base of walls, turrets and mechanoids near your colony. It arrives asleep and wakes when you come close, when you damage it, or when a timer runs out. The mechanoids never leave, so you choose when and how to fight.

li.heading: What lands
li.text: With Royalty, clusters can appear once raid points reach 400. A cluster has walls, turrets and unstable power cells, and may carry condition causers such as sun blockers or EMP dynamos. Auto charge turrets guard it; they are always hostile and never need rearming. The mechanoids stay until they are destroyed.

table.li: Proximity activator | A human comes within about 13 tiles
Activator on a timer | Enough time has passed
Damage | Any part of it takes damage
Construction | Anything is built within 2 tiles of a mechanoid or mech building

li.heading: Taking it apart
li.text: Leave it asleep until you are ready, and keep colonists, haulers and blueprints well clear. Then shell it from out of its range with mortars; EMP shells are best against mechanoids. Without mortars, prepare a fallback line before it wakes, because some clusters wake on a timer whatever you do.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: infestations
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Insect hives that grow under warm, dark mountain rock
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Overhead mountain stops drop pods and shells, and it is also where insects nest.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Insects can burrow up under overhead mountain near your colony and build hives that keep spreading. Every mountain base carries this risk. Walls or deep cold can make your rock almost insect-proof.

li.heading: Where insects can spawn
li.text: A natural infestation needs a spot that is all of these:

points.li: Under overhead mountain
Warmer than -17 °C
Within 30 tiles of your buildings
Not inside a 1×1 enclosed space

li.after: Insects prefer dark areas far from open sky, and below -8 °C the chance gradually drops. Deep drilling can also bring insects, with no hives and no mountain needed. With Biotech, wastepack infestations hatch from stasis cocoons.

li.heading: How often, how big
li.text: Random infestations come at most once every 20 days, and never once the map has 30 or more hives. Their size scales with raid points, and left alone, an infestation grows past 30 hives.

li.heading: Insect-proofing the rock
li.text:
Only walls stop spawns; doors and columns don't. A wall on every second tile is enough, because a valid spot needs more than 1×1 of open mountain. Wall off or fill unused mountain space, including old mining tunnels, and don't dig out more mountain than you need. Light the mountain rooms you use and keep them close to open sky where you can.
With power, you can instead keep every overhead-mountain tile at or below -17 °C with coolers, but a solar flare breaks this, so walls are safer. Without power you can't freeze the rock, so build walls.
When hives do appear, fight them from a doorway at range. Insect bites carry a high infection risk.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: toxic fallout
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Days of poison from the sky: stay under a roof
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Every hour outdoors during fallout adds to toxic buildup.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Toxic fallout poisons everything outdoors for days. Pawns build up toxins, outdoor crops wither, and long exposure can leave permanent brain damage or cancer. The fix is to roof the walkways, the workplaces and the barn.

li.heading: People outdoors
li.text:
Fallout lasts 2.5 to 10.5 days. It never comes before day 60 and has a 90-day cooldown. Pawns outside build toxic buildup at 40% per day, and being outdoors during fallout costs -5 mood. From 40% buildup, about 24 hours outside, there is a risk of permanent dementia or carcinoma; 100% kills. Animals have 50% toxic resistance, and insects and mechanoids are immune. With Biotech, a face mask gives +50% and a gas mask +80% toxic environment resistance.
Build roofed walkways between the places people work, and set an allowed area that stays under roofs. Pull anyone whose buildup reaches "moderate" indoors and keep them there.

li.heading: Crops and animals
li.text: All outdoor plants wither except anima trees, anima grass, Gauranlen trees and pods, and polux trees. Roofed crops survive, but rot without a sun lamp, so keep a backup sun lamp over a roofed field to go on growing food. Without sun lamps, harvest whatever is ready when the fallout starts, eat from your preserved stores and keep animals in a roofed barn.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: solar flares
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Every powered device stops, for up to half a day
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Campfires, fueled stoves and torches keep working through a solar flare.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A solar flare shuts down every powered device on the map: lights, benches, coolers, turrets and hydroponics. It doesn't last long, but a warming freezer and silent turrets at the wrong moment can cost you food or colonists.

li.heading: What stops, and the backup for each
li.text: A flare lasts 0.15 to 0.5 days and can't be prevented in the base game. Unpowered devices are immune, so a tribal colony can ignore flares until its first powered building goes up. Everyone else needs an unpowered backup for what matters most:

table.li: The freezer stops cooling | A double-walled freezer that holds the cold, with food frozen promptly after collecting it
Powered work buildings stop | Wood-fueled versions, such as a fueled stove and fueled smithy
A greenhouse loses its heat | One campfire in the room, lit only when needed, which can keep it warm at -40 °C outside

li.after: Passive coolers can't go below 17 °C, so they won't save a freezer. Soil crops in a greenhouse survive a power cut if they stay warm, so the cold is the real danger there. With Biotech, combat mechs may wander when band nodes are off.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: heat waves and cold snaps
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: A few days of brutal temperature, and how to ride them out
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Heat waves hit the freezer hardest; cold snaps hit crops and anyone working outside.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A heat wave pushes temperatures up to 17 °C higher for a few days; a cold snap drops them by 20 °C. Both threaten people working outside, the freezer and the crops. With coolers, heaters and warm clothes ready in advance, neither does much harm.

table.li: Only where | Summers go above 20 °C | Summer temperatures sit between 0 and 15 °C

li.heading: In a heat wave
li.text:
The freezer is the first thing at risk. Set two electric coolers to different temperatures, such as -5 °C and -10 °C, so one can idle, and double-wall the freezer.
Without power, put passive coolers in bedrooms and work rooms to keep people out of heatstroke. Passive coolers only work in an enclosed room and can't cool below 17 °C.

li.heading: In a cold snap
li.text: Crops begin dying at -10 °C, so harvest exposed crops that are at least 65% grown. Light campfires or heaters indoors, and make jackets, dusters or parkas for anyone who works outside. Stock haygrass or kibble for the animals before the cold comes; simple meals can feed any animal except wargs.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: eclipse and volcanic winter
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: When the sun goes dim for a day, or for a whole season
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: An eclipse leaves solar panels nearly useless for about a day.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: An eclipse darkens the sky for about a day: solar panels barely work and outdoor crops slow down. A volcanic winter is the long version, with weeks of dimmer and colder days. Neither kills plants outright, but the cold and empty batteries can.

li.heading: Eclipse
li.text: An eclipse lasts 0.75 to 1.25 days and has a 15-day cooldown. Solar panels barely work and outdoor crops grow slightly slower. With Ideology, an eclipse only affects mood under the eclipse precept.

li.heading: Volcanic winter
li.text: A volcanic winter lasts 7.5 to 40 days. It never comes before day 60 and has a 140-day cooldown. Plants grow slower, solar output falls and temperatures drop. Sources disagree on how dark it gets: one says daylight falls to 86% of normal, another describes 30% less light and a 7 °C drop.

li.heading: Power and food through the dark
li.text:
Don't rely on solar alone. Add wind, wood-fired, chemfuel or geothermal power, plus extra batteries. Heated, lit greenhouses keep food growing through a volcanic winter.
A tribal colony has no solar power to lose. Watch the crops and stock fuel for the colder weeks.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: fire safety
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Build in stone, keep firebreaks and catch fires early
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Stone walls don't burn, but whatever is stored against them still can.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Fire races through wooden walls, wooden floors and anything stored on them. Most colony fires start at a generator, a battery, a campfire or a stray incendiary. Build important rooms from stone and have a way to put fires out before they reach the stockpile.

li.heading: How fire spreads
li.text:
Items and structures ignite above 235 °C. Embers travel up to 2 tiles, so firebreaks should be 2 tiles wide. Items on stone shelves can still burn.
Burning deals 2 heat damage per second however big the flames, ignoring armor penetration. Heat-resistant clothing such as devilstrand helps.

li.heading: Putting fires out
li.text: Fires are put out by colonists beating them, by firefoam, by rain on unroofed tiles and by explosions. Colonists only fight fires inside the home area unless drafted, so make the home area cover the whole base. Firefoam comes from three places:
li.after: Firefoam needs the Electricity research first; on a tribal start the Firefoam research costs 1,200.

li.heading: Building against it
li.text:
Build walls from stone or other non-flammable materials, above all around generators, batteries and kitchens. Put generators and batteries on stone floors, and a firefoam popper in rooms with valuable stock or power equipment.
Without firefoam, rely on stone walls, stone floors under campfires and torches, 2-tile firebreaks and plenty of colonists set to firefight.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: short circuits and batteries
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Why batteries explode, and how to make them stop
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: One short circuit can drain your batteries and start a fire.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A short circuit ("Zzztt") starts a fire and can drain your batteries in a single blast. In recent versions you can almost rule it out with hidden conduits and roofed batteries. Until your wiring is safe, keep the batteries in a stone room where a fire has nowhere to go.

li.heading: What causes a short
li.text: "Zzztt" is a random bad event with an 8-day cooldown. It comes from regular power conduits and from batteries that aren't roofed, and it causes fires and drained batteries. Powered buildings and appliances can also short out in rain or snow, and shorts caused by rain or snow ignore the cooldown. Since version 1.5, hidden conduits and roofed batteries prevent it.

li.heading: A safe battery room

points.li: Use hidden conduits.
Roof every battery.
Build batteries in pairs, away from generators and never on wood, so at most two go up at once.
Put a firefoam popper in the room.

li.after: A battery stores 600 Wd, charges at 50% efficiency and loses 5 Wd a day. A colony without power has nothing to short out, but plan the battery room before the first battery goes in.
